5785.etyen:
From bibel (“Bible”) + ordbok (“dictionary”), literally “Bible dictionary”.
The first element is ultimately from Latin biblia (“the Bible; books”), from Ancient Greek βιβλία (biblía, “books”), the plural of βιβλίον (biblíon, “small book”), a diminutive of βίβλος (bíblos, “book, papyrus scroll”), from βύβλος (búblos, “papyrus”). The second element is ordbok (“dictionary”), probably modelled on Wörterbuch (“dictionary”) and synchronically ord (“word”) + bok (“book”). ord is from Old Norse orð (“word”), from Proto-Germanic *wurdą (“word, speech”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”), itsel

Portugal is a country in southern Europe. It lies on the Atlantic Ocean, on the western side of the Iberian Peninsula, and borders Spain to the north and east.

1000089.etyen:
Borrowed from Portuguese Portugal (“Portugal”). The Portuguese name continues Old Galician-Portuguese Portugal, from Late Latin Portucale, a univerbation of Portus Cale (“Port of Cale”), a Roman place-name associated with the area of present-day Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia.
The first element is portus (“harbour, port”), from Proto-Italic *portus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing, passage”). The origin of Cale is uncertain, though a Celtic origin has been proposed.
Cognates and parallel forms include Norwegian Nynorsk Portugal, Danish Portugal, Swedish Portugal, German Por

1000601.etyen:
Internationalism, ultimately from Latin Aethiopia, from Ancient Greek Αἰθιοπία (Aithiopía), from Αἰθίοψ (Aithíops, “Ethiopian”) + -ία (-ía).
The Ancient Greek name originally had a much broader geographical application than the name of the modern country, referring to peoples and lands south of Egypt. The name later became associated with the Ethiopian highlands and the states developing there. The same Greek name was borrowed into Ge'ez ኢትዮጵያ (ʾityop̣ya) and Amharic ኢትዮጵያ (ʾityop̣ya, “Ethiopia”).

1000857.etyen: Inherited from Old Norse Gloppi, originally the name of the fjord now called Gloppefjorden. The name is probably related to Old Norse gloppa, the source of gloppe (“narrow opening; cleft, ravine”), and likely refers to the fjord's narrow mouth between Anda and Hestenesøyra. The surname is habitational, from the place name.

en.g: Used to form female given names, especially from male given names and, less commonly, from other female given names

1001113.etyen:
Borrowed from Danish -ine (“female name-forming suffix”). The Danish name-forming pattern was introduced from France through Germany and ultimately continues Latin -īna (“feminine form of -īnus”), the feminine of -īnus (“of or pertaining to”). The pattern first occurred in upper-class naming before becoming highly productive in Danish and Norwegian female-name formation, particularly during the 19th century.
Compare Swedish -ina and English -ine (“female name-forming suffix”).

en.g: a female given name from Old Norse

1001369.etyen:
Derived from Old Norse Álfhildr, from álfr (“elf”) + hildr (“battle, strife”). The spelling Alfhild was revived through Jacob Aall’s 1838 Norwegian translation of Snorri Sturluson’s kings' sagas.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Alfhild, Swedish Alfhild, Danish Alfhild, Icelandic Álfhildur and Faroese Álvhild (“female given name”).

en.g: a female given name from Latin [in turn from Old High German, in turn from Proto-Germanic], equivalent to English Ottilie

1004697.etyen:
One of several Norwegian spellings of a female given name going back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending. The spelling with th is historical and does not represent a separate /θ/ sound in Norwegian.
Compare Danish Othelia, Swedish Othelia, German Ottilie and English Ottilie (“female given name”).

1004953.etyen:
Grønland (“Greenland”) + hare (“hare”), with linking -s-, literally “Greenland hare”. The first element, Grønland (“Greenland”), is from Old Norse Grǿnland (“Greenland”), itself grǿnn (“green”) + land (“land”), literally “green land”. Old Norse grǿnn (“green”) is from Proto-Germanic *grōniz (“green”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”), while land (“land”) is from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”).
